title: How to End a Sermon So It Lands
subtitle: How to write a sermon conclusion that lands, with practical guidance on the call, the final image, and leaving weight instead of tidy resolution.

sections.title: Most Sermons Die in the Last Two Minutes
sections.body:
You can do everything right for thirty minutes and lose it all in the final two.

The conclusion is where good sermons go to die. The preacher has spent his energy on the body, the introduction got the attention, and the ending arrives as an afterthought. So he circles. He restates. He says in conclusion and then preaches four more minutes. He says and finally three separate times. The room, which was with him, begins to gather coats in its mind. The landing he needed becomes a slow taxi to a gate that never comes.

This is not a small thing. The end is what they carry to the car. It is the part that follows them into the week, the sentence that surfaces on Wednesday when the marriage is hard or the diagnosis comes. A sermon that does not land does not stay. You worked all week to say one true thing. The conclusion is where you make sure it has somewhere to live.

sections.title: Make the Call Specific or Do Not Make It
sections.body:
Every sermon asks something of the people. Vague asks change no one.

The weak conclusion ends in fog. Let us be more loving this week. Let us trust God more. Let us walk closer with him. No one resists this because no one can act on it. It is too large to obey and too soft to refuse, so it slides off. The call must be specific enough that a person could fail at it. That is the test. If it cannot be failed, it cannot be obeyed.

So name the thing. Not love your family more, but go home and tell your son the words your father never told you. Not forgive, but pick up the phone you have been avoiding for two years. Not trust God, but stop checking the account balance as if it were your savior. The specific call costs the preacher something too, because specific means somebody in the room is convicted and somebody is uncomfortable and you cannot hide behind a generality. Good. That discomfort is the text doing its work. Do not rescue them from it.

sections.title: Leave Weight, Do Not Resolve It
sections.body:
The instinct to tie a bow at the end is the instinct to disarm the text. Resist it.

We were trained to resolve. To end with comfort, to send them out lighter than they came, to make sure no one leaves troubled. But the texts do not always resolve, and when you force a resolution they never intended, you teach the people that God always lands soft. Then comes the week when life does not land soft, and the soft God you preached is no help at all.

The better ending names what remains. It does not pretend the tension is gone. It lets the people walk out carrying something. The prodigal came home, but the older brother is still standing in the yard, and the story ends with him out there in the dark, and Jesus does not tell us whether he went in. That is on purpose. Sometimes the most faithful thing you can do is stop talking while the weight is still in the room. Do not answer every question. Do not soften every edge. End where the text ends, even when it ends in the dark, and trust that the Spirit can carry a sentence further than you can.

sections.title: End on an Image, Not an Argument
sections.body:
The mind forgets propositions. It keeps pictures.

If your last move is a summary of your three points, you have ended on the part most easily forgotten. The argument was the road. The road is not the destination. Land them somewhere they can stand, a single concrete image that holds the whole sermon in one frame. The father running down the road with his robe gathered in his fists. The empty tomb at dawn. The hand reaching down into the water for a man who could not save himself.

This is not decoration. An image is a handle. It gives the truth something to be carried by. Weeks later they will not recall your outline, but they will recall the picture, and the picture will carry the truth back to them at the moment they need it.

So write the last sentence first if you have to. Know where you are landing before you take off. The conclusion is not the place to discover what you think. It is the place to deliver, in the fewest words you have used all day, the one thing you came to say.

sections.title: The Mechanics of a Clean Landing
sections.body:
A clean ending is mostly a matter of nerve. You have to be willing to stop.

Decide before you stand up where the sermon ends, and write that ending in full. Do not improvise the last two minutes. The improvised ending is the one that circles, because a tired preacher with no script will always reach for one more thing. Have the final sentence on the page. Say it. Then close your mouth.

Watch for the false endings. The sermon that ends three times has trained the room to disbelieve the ending. When you signal the close, mean it. No new point after the call. No fresh illustration after the image. If it was important, it belonged in the body. The conclusion is for landing, not for loading.

And lower your voice. The young preacher thinks the climax must be loud. Often the most powerful ending is the quietest, the volume dropping until the room has to lean in to catch the last words. Then silence. Let it sit. Do not rush to pray it away. The weight you leave in that silence is the sermon they take home. Stop while it is still heavy.
